newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai banks seen paring rates to boost lending.
newsitem.headline: Thai banks seen paring rates to boost lending.

text.p: Thai banks are seen cutting high lending rates by 25-50 basis points by the year's end to boost sluggish lending activity, bankers and analysts said on Tuesday.

"Lending by most commercial banks was very slow in the first half and much lower than targeted. This will partly prompt banks to cut interest rates by 25-50 basis points during the rest of the year," Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, told Reuters.
Domestic lending rates at most Thai banks range from 13.25-13.75 percent, among the highest in Southeast Asia.
According to Bank of Thailand (BOT) data, total credit extension in the first half of the year was about 100 million baht (US$4 million) lower than its estimate of 350 billion.
The central bank also said it expects growth in domestic lending for the whole year to be 19 percent above that in 1995, but down from an earlier target of 21 percent.
Analysts attributed this slowdown to a cooling of Thailand's exports and economy.
The BOT forecast last month that Thai exports and gross domestic product would grow by 10.2 and 7.8 percent, respectively, below its previous estimates of 17.4 and 8.3 percent.
Charl Kengchon, head of money and banking at Thai Farmers Research Co Ltd, also expects bank lending rates to drop by 25-50 basis points.

"But I don't think lending rates will decline below 13 percent if the deposit rate is still at 9.00 percent. Banks want to maintain their spread of about 4.00 percentage points between lending and deposit rates," he said.
Analysts said a key factor that could prevent further reductions in local lending rates was any heavy outflow of foreign funds as this would tighten liquidity.

"If there is no major occurrence to stimulate a heavy outflow of foreign funds in the remaining four months (of 1996), lending rates will have room to fall further," said Satian Tantanasarit, vice-president at Thai Danu Bank.
Singapore-based Paribas Capital Market said in a report on Thailand that it expected rates to ease by 100-125 basis points by the year-end, bringing the minimum loan rate to around 12 percent.
"We expect the downtrend in interest rates to continue through the second half," Paribas said.
Foreigners have parked large sums of money in Thailand to cash in on on high interest rates, buying baht and placing the money in deposit accounts and/or local bills of exchange.

In recent days foreign outflows have been quite heavy as foreigners remain worried about the domestic political and economic situation and the stock market has been sluggish, analysts said. They gave no details.

Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa faces a no-confidence debate, tentatively set for September 18. His six-party coalition has become bogged down by political infighting and this has raised concerns about the stability of his administration, political analysts said.
